loc:buchhandlung-vorwald-0.name: Buchhandlung Vorwald
loc:buchhandlung-vorwald-0.description: Shelves lean overhead on every side; a bell on the door and dust in the window-light.

loc:buchhandlung-vorwald-1.name: Buchhandlung Vorwald
loc:buchhandlung-vorwald-1.description: A cat sleeps on the ledger; the proprietor peers over half-moon glasses and names a price without looking up.

loc:gloria-kino-2.name: Gloria-Kino
loc:gloria-kino-2.description: The back rows are kept for courting couples and anyone who would rather watch the door than the picture.

loc:landungssteg-treustra-e-3.name: Landungssteg Treustraße
loc:landungssteg-treustra-e-3.description: Coal dust blackens the cobbles; a crane swings a net of crates overhead and no one below so much as glances up.

loc:legation-of-the-free-republic-4.name: Legation of the Free Republic
loc:legation-of-the-free-republic-4.description: High-ceilinged rooms smelling of floor wax and sealing wax, telephones ringing behind closed doors.

loc:heuriger-grinzinger-hof-5.name: Heuriger Grinzinger Hof
loc:heuriger-grinzinger-hof-5.description: Jugs of cloudy young wine come and go; the talk runs loud and the faces blur pleasantly in the lamplight.

loc:the-marmorbar-at-hotel-donaublick-6.name: the Marmorbar at Hotel Donaublick
loc:the-marmorbar-at-hotel-donaublick-6.description: A revolving door spills in a draught of street cold each time a new party arrives already half an argument in.

loc:cafe-hochquell-7.name: Café Hochquell
loc:cafe-hochquell-7.description: A marble-topped corner where a man can nurse one small black coffee for a whole afternoon and be left in peace.

loc:cafe-sperl-garten-8.name: Café Sperl­garten
loc:cafe-sperl-garten-8.description: A high room of marble tables and bentwood chairs, thick with coffee steam and cigarette smoke.

loc:bezirksbucherei-alsergrund-9.name: Bezirksbücherei Alsergrund
loc:bezirksbucherei-alsergrund-9.description: Card catalogues wall the entrance; readers turn pages under a ceiling stained by decades of lamp-smoke.

loc:bezirksbucherei-alsergrund-10.name: Bezirksbücherei Alsergrund
loc:bezirksbucherei-alsergrund-10.description: Students and pensioners share the long tables in silence, each walled off behind a rampart of borrowed books.

loc:viktor-adler-markt-11.name: Viktor-Adler-Markt
loc:viktor-adler-markt-11.description: By mid-afternoon the barrows are half empty and the sweepers move in; a few traders argue over the unsold stock.

loc:augarten-12.name: Augarten
loc:augarten-12.description: Children feed the ducks at the pond while nursemaids compare notes on a bench and miss nothing that passes.

loc:sudbahnhof-13.name: Südbahnhof
loc:sudbahnhof-13.description: Benches of waiting travellers, a left-luggage office, and a kiosk where you can watch the whole concourse.

loc:wohnung-gro-e-sperlgasse-14.name: Wohnung Große Sperlgasse
loc:wohnung-gro-e-sperlgasse-14.description: Dust sheets over the furniture of someone long gone; the place smells of cold ash and other people's absence.

loc:the-station-15.name: the Station
loc:the-station-15.description: A floor of locked offices behind an unmarked door: steel cabinets, a cipher room, and a teleprinter chattering.

loc:tabak-trafik-weinhuber-16.name: Tabak-Trafik Weinhuber
loc:tabak-trafik-weinhuber-16.description: A narrow booth that smells of tobacco and newsprint, its shutter half-down against the wind.

loc:the-corner-of-wiedner-hauptstra-e-17.name: the corner of Wiedner Hauptstraße
loc:the-corner-of-wiedner-hauptstra-e-17.description: A clanging red tram slows at the kerb; the waiting crowd shuffles and reforms as it pulls away.

loc:the-corner-of-mariahilfer-stra-e-18.name: the corner of Mariahilfer Straße
loc:the-corner-of-mariahilfer-stra-e-18.description: The overhead wires spark blue at the junction; the crowd leans out to look up the street for the next car.

loc:zollfreilager-nord-19.name: Zollfreilager Nord
loc:zollfreilager-nord-19.description: Stencilled crates bound for a dozen cities crowd the loading bay, their consignee names half painted out.

The handling officer reviews a sketch of the registry room passed up through a cut-out.
A front clears a debt for a registry clerk, who then begins meeting the handling officer at a quiet kaffeehaus.
A wireless operator logs a new recognition signal for the recruited clerk in the night schedule.
The clerk swaps the cipher component for a duplicate blank during a thin afternoon shift and leaves it at a dead drop.
A street courier recovers the drop and signals the lift is clean.
A dock worker carries the component in a goods crate across the sector boundary on an early-morning barge.
A watcher confirms the crate clears the river checkpoint without a search.
The trader collects the week's notes from a tobacconist kiosk, the bundle slipped across the counter with the newspapers.
A watcher clocks the trader working his chits over a café table and takes the shorthand for cipher.
A hotel porter carries the hollowed guidebook across the sector line on his afternoon off, bundle and all.
The porter hands the trader his takings at the hotel bar, the pair careful never to be seen counting.
Clients come to the kiosk to change their scrip, each leaving with a thinner envelope than they hoped.
An émigré fixer, hearing of the ring, passes a quiet word to a contact — nothing to do with any service.

doc:public-text/almanac-vienna-household.title: The Household Almanac and Register for the Year
doc:public-text/almanac-vienna-household.body:
The almanac opens with a word on the seasons and the work each one asks of a careful household.
In the first month the days are short and the river runs cold under a grey and heavy sky.
A prudent family lays in coal early, mends what the autumn wore thin, and keeps the lamp trimmed against the long evening.
The second month brings a thaw that is not to be trusted, for the frost returns by night and the streets turn to glass before dawn.
By the third month the market stalls show the first green of the year and the price of eggs begins at last to fall.
In spring the gardener turns the beds, sows the early roots, and watches the almanac for the days the moon favours planting.
The fourth month is the month of rain, when the gutters run and the washing will not dry, and patience is the only remedy.
High summer fills the orchards along the slow bend of the river and the evenings grow long and warm and full of dust.
A good cook preserves in the seventh month what the eighth month will not keep, and labels every jar in a plain and honest hand.
Autumn is the season of accounts, when the wise settle their debts before the cold and reckon the year that is closing.
The ninth month brings the fairs, the harvest home, and the first fires lit against the evening chill.
By the tenth month the leaves are down, the barges run low in the water, and the fog sits on the river until midday.
The eleventh month asks the household to look to its stores, its boots and its roof before the true winter comes.
In the last month the year turns inward, the days are shortest, and the family gathers close about the single warm room.
A table of weights and measures follows, for the market, the kitchen and the yard, that no honest trader be cheated.
A pound is reckoned here in the old manner and again in the new, that buyer and seller may agree before the scale is read.
The register of fairs lists the spring cattle fair, the midsummer cloth fair, the autumn produce fair and the winter market by the old gate.
Each fair opens at the eighth hour and closes when the light fails, and no stall may be struck before the bell.
A note on the post advises that letters within the city are collected twice daily and that parcels require a stamp of the proper weight.
The office of the district magistrate keeps its hours from the ninth hour to the fourth, and is closed upon the day of rest.
The ration office opens early and the queue forms earlier still, so the almanac counsels the reader to carry a book and a patient temper.
A page of household remedies offers honey for the throat, chamomile for the nerves, and a hot brick wrapped in flannel for the cold bed.
The almanac warns against the quack and the pedlar of miracle cures, and recommends instead rest, broth and the plain advice of a sober physician.
A column of sayings reminds the reader that a stitch in time saves nine, that the early bird takes the worm, and that a watched pot is slow to boil.
The gardener's calendar names the days to prune, the days to sow and the days to leave the beds alone and trust the weather.
A table of the tides on the great rivers follows, for those whose trade rides the water from the mountains to the sea.
The almanac closes its first part with a prayer for a mild winter, a kind harvest and a quiet year at the crossing posts.
The second part is given over to the register of the city and the plain facts a householder should keep near the door.
The city stands upon the river where the plain meets the last of the hills, and has stood there, by the chronicles, a very long time.
Its streets are laid in rings about an old inner town, and a broad avenue circles where the walls once ran before they were pulled down.
The water is drawn from the mountains by a long aqueduct and is counted among the sweetest a city ever drank.
The markets gather by district, each on its appointed day, and the almanac prints the days in order that no cook arrive to a shuttered square.
The register of weights for bread fixes the honest loaf, and the baker who sells short is named to the magistrate and fined.
A short history of the almanac itself boasts that it has been printed every year, through hard winters and lean ones, without a single year missed.
The printer thanks the reader, commends the almanac to the household shelf, and promises a corrected and enlarged edition when the year comes round again.
A final page of blank ruled lines invites the family to keep its own accounts, its birthdays and its small triumphs, against the almanac's own.

doc:public-text/anthology-river-and-ston.title: The River and the Stone — A Reader's Anthology
doc:public-text/anthology-river-and-ston.body:
This small anthology gathers verse and prose for the quiet hour. The pieces are new, written for the common reader, and ask only to be read slowly and without hurry.
Morning on the Water
The river wakes before the town,
a slow grey ribbon under cloud,
it carries off the night downstream
and will not speak of it aloud.
The barges nose against the quay,
the lamps go out along the shore,
and someone whistles, far away,
a tune I think I knew before.
The Keeper of the Bridge
There was once a man whose whole work was to watch a bridge, and he knew every plank of it as a reader knows a page. He counted the carts at dawn and the walkers at dusk, and he could tell by the sound of a step whether the one who crossed was tired or in a hurry or afraid. People thought his work was small, but he knew that a bridge is only as safe as the eyes that keep it, and he was proud, in his quiet way, of the hundred crossings that passed each day without a stumble.
The Lamp in the Window
A lamp set in a window
is a small and steady thing,
it says the house is waking,
it says the kettle sings.
It does not ask the weather,
it does not fear the night,
it keeps its one plain promise
to hold a little light.
A Letter Never Sent
I meant to write to you in the autumn, when the leaves came down along the avenue and the air turned sharp and clean. I meant to tell you that the old cafe still keeps your corner table, that the waiter still remembers how you took your coffee, and that the city, for all its changes, has not quite let you go. But the autumn passed, and the winter after it, and the letter stayed on my desk, half written, as letters so often do. I send it now, late and plain, because a thing said late is better than a thing not said.
Market Day
The square fills up at the eighth hour,
with baskets, boots and bargaining,
the cheese is weighed, the apples turned,
and sparrows watch for anything.
A clock strikes somewhere over roofs,
the crowd thins out, the stalls come down,
and quiet settles on the stones
like dusk that gathers in a town.
The Clockmaker's Patience
The clockmaker worked by a single window, and he said that patience was the only tool he could not buy. A spring will not be hurried, he told me, and a wheel that is forced will break. You set each piece in its place and you wait, and when it is right the clock keeps time of its own accord and asks nothing further of you. I have thought since that a great many things are like his clocks, and that most of our troubles come of forcing the wheel.
Snow in the Inner Town
The snow comes down on the inner town
and softens every hard-edged thing,
it hushes carts, it hoods the lamps,
it muffles even the quarter's ring.
A child draws letters in the white,
a dog goes nosing down the lane,
and for an hour the oldest streets
are new and clean and strange again.
What the Ferryman Knew
The ferryman had crossed the same stretch of water for forty years, and he said the river taught a man to read the weather better than any almanac. He knew the colour the sky took before a storm, the smell the wind carried off the hills, the way the current pulled when the thaw was coming. He had never left the valley, and he did not wish to; the whole world, he said, passed over his ferry in time, and he had only to wait and watch and work the oars, and the world would show him all it had.
The anthology closes here. The reader who has come this far is thanked, and wished a quiet evening and a kind morning after it.
